title: Gunbarrel Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Gunbarrel wells have a 35-foot median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and finished well costs of $7,800-$14,400.
h1: Gunbarrel, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Gunbarrel sits in a part of Boulder County where nearby well records vary sharply by location and aquifer. The local permit data shows many shallow wells, dependable reported yields in the middle of the range, and a large number of permits tied to fractured bedrock or Denver Basin aquifers.

That makes the well record worth checking before you buy land or plan a home. A nearby permit can help set expectations, but it does not guarantee the same depth, water level, or production on your parcel. The final answer comes from a site-specific permit review, drilling conditions, casing and grout requirements, and a properly tested well.

sections.heading: Gunbarrel well depth depends on the ground beneath the lot
sections.html:
Among permitted wells within five miles of Gunbarrel, the median reported depth is 35 feet. The middle half runs from 20 to 160 feet, so a driller’s bid based only on the median could be misleading. Two-thirds of the recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 26% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 8% are between 300 and 600 feet, and none are recorded above 600 feet in that depth mix.

The deepest well on record reaches 3,000 feet, showing how much local conditions can vary despite the shallow median. Permits name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers most often, with alluvial and Laramie Fox Hills wells also present. Denver Basin aquifer wells account for 39% of the records.

sections.heading: What Gunbarrel wells produce for household use
sections.html:
Reported pump yield has a 10.0 gallons-per-minute median, with the middle half between 7.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. That is a useful planning range for a typical household, but it is not the same as storage in the well or guaranteed daily supply. Only 419 wells report a pump yield, so the available test data is a subset of the full permit record.

Most reported wells fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, representing 63% of yield records. Another 26% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Low production is less common but still important: 9% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 2% report under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the pump test and recovery information, not just the permit.

sections.heading: Gunbarrel water levels show a shallower recent pattern
sections.html:
The median static water level is 12 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 8 and 24 feet. That shallow water level can simplify pumping, but it also means the water is relatively close to surface conditions. Proper casing, grout, surface drainage, and septic placement matter.

The decade figures do not show a dropping water table in these records. Median depth to water was 20 feet in the 1950s and 1960s, 14 feet in the 2010s, and 10 feet in the 2020s. Treat that as a pattern in reported measurements, not a promise for one parcel. Water levels can vary with location, season, pumping, and the aquifer used.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers around Gunbarrel
sections.html:
The records include 3,968 permitted wells, with 2,300 recorded as constructed. Domestic or household use makes up 52% of the use mix; monitoring wells account for 31%, followed by stock and irrigation wells. The newest permit year is 2025, so the area continues to have current permitting activity rather than being represented only by older wells.

The most frequently listed drillers are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Waneka & Son Drilling (Waneka, Don), and Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.). Their appearance in the records is useful local context, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, scope, references, and the proposed casing, grout, testing, and abandonment terms before hiring anyone.

sections.heading: Gunbarrel drilling cost starts with depth, not the whole project
sections.html:
For the Denver Basin sedimentary-bedrock conditions used in the local cost model, a typical drilling rate is $50 to $70 per foot. At the 35-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $1,800 to $2,400. That is only the drilling portion and should not be treated as the finished water-system price.

A completed well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $7,800 to $14,400. A bid can move outside that range when the actual formation requires more depth, specialized casing, difficult access, longer utility runs, or different treatment and storage equipment. Get the driller to separate depth assumptions from pump, tank, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit costs.

sections.heading: Checks that matter before building near Gunbarrel
sections.html:
Low yield is the main water-supply risk to investigate, even though the median reported yield is 10.0 gallons per minute. A dry hole or a well that produces less than expected can change the entire project budget. Fractured-bedrock wells are especially unpredictable because water may depend on narrow fractures rather than a uniform layer.

Environmental records also deserve review. Within about ten miles, the map includes 435 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 186 historic mine features, and 19 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These records do not prove contamination on a specific lot, but they support ordering a complete water-quality test. Check septic setbacks, available building area, access for a rig, and the legal water use allowed by the DWR permit. Exempt household-use wells still have a 35 gpm pumping limit, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: A practical lot review for Gunbarrel buyers
sections.html:
Before closing, compare the subject parcel with nearby permits in Gunbarrel, Niwot, Valmont, Leyner, Boulder, Lafayette, and Paragon Estates. Focus on wells in the same geologic setting rather than relying on the nearest record. Look for reported depth, yield, static water level, construction details, and the permitted use.

For a new build, have a Colorado water-rights professional confirm the permit path before design is finalized. Then have a driller review rig access, likely depth, casing and grout, pump sizing, trench routes, and testing. Plan the septic system and house location around well protection and required setbacks. Tri-Lakes Contracting can help with access driveways, site development, new-build septic systems, and custom homes as a licensed Colorado contractor, but the well permit and water-quality decisions should be handled with the appropriate water professionals.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Gunbarrel, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Gunbarrel is 35 feet. The middle half of records runs from 20 to 160 feet, and 66% are under 100 feet. Conditions still vary widely: the deepest recorded well reaches 3,000 feet, so nearby permits should be reviewed by aquifer and location before assuming a shallow well will work on a specific lot.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Gunbarrel?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $70 per foot for drilling in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 35-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $1,800 to $2,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $7,800 to $14,400. Actual bids depend on depth, access, construction, and utility runs.

faq.q: How much water does a Gunbarrel well produce?
faq.a: Reported wells near Gunbarrel have a 10.0 gallons-per-minute median yield, with the middle half between 7.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. About 63% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 2% report under 1 gallon per minute. Only 419 wells include yield data, so request a pump test for the specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Gunbarrel?
faq.a: A permit or nearby yield record does not establish drinking-water safety. The area has 435 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 186 historic mine features, and 19 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about ten miles. Those mapped sites are not proof of contamination on your lot, but they make a complete laboratory water-quality test an important buying step.

faq.q: Are Gunbarrel well water levels going down?
faq.a: The reported decade pattern does not show a dropping water table. Median static water depth was 20 feet in the 1950s and 1960s, 14 feet in the 2010s, and 10 feet in the 2020s. The overall median is 12 feet, with the middle half from 8 to 24 feet. Individual levels can still vary by location, season, and pumping.
